You shall carry a dog's tongue placed in your shoe beneath your thumb, or if you carry a dried dog's heart with you, according to Sextus. Use hare hair or dung, according to Pliny. Or carry a young weasel's severed tail on your foot, or give a frog to the dog in a morsel of food; all these things are to avoid the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that a man who removes a tick from a pig and carries it for a while will cause dogs to flee from his sight all day long. Oppian writes:

> If you carry a small piece cut from a hyena's hide,
> Immediately the fierce puppies and dogs
> Stunned with bitter terror, will not bark at you
> As you walk by, even if they had barked before.

### How to prevent a dog from running.

If you smear its wings with oil, it will be hindered in running; it will happen in this way.

### How to make a hawk spirited.

You will animate a bird against its prey so that it attacks large birds. Moisten the food it uses at the time of hunting with wine; or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you wish it to fly, give it three morsels of meat soaked in wine, or pour wine from its beak into a dove chick, then make it fly. Thus:

### You will make partridges more combative,

If you give them twigs of maidenhair fern <term>adiantum</term> <gloss>maidenhair fern</gloss> in their food, according to Pliny, and:

### Roosters become more combative,

By giving them garlic in their food just before they are to fight, from which the term <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlic-fed</gloss> is most wittily used in ancient comedy for one who is fierce and overly inclined to battle.

### So that a bird does not fly high.

Pluck out the tail feathers that direct its course upward, and it will fly in a circle down below. If you wish:

### That a bird cannot fly at all.

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing; it remains without harm, but the bird will not fly. In this way, they do not fly away in aviaries.

The method of that citrination which is perfected by <term>Vitriol</term> <gloss>a sulfate mineral</gloss> or <term>Cuperosa</term> <gloss>copper sulfate/vitriol</gloss> is as follows. Let a certain quantity of each of these be taken, and let that part which is capable of sublimation be sublimed until it is sublimed with total expression. After this, let what has been sublimed be sublimed again with the appropriate degree of fire, so that something from it is fixed after something else, until the greater part of it is fixed. Afterwards, let it be administered with the caution of fire, so that a greater fire may be administered to it for perfection. After this, let it be dissolved into a most ruby-red water, to which there is no equal. Then, you shall devise a way to provide it with entry into the Lunar body <note>the body of silver</note>, and these devices have been sufficiently shown to you if you are an inquirer of the perfect work which we have written. And because we see that things of this kind adhere amicably to the depth of the Moon, we have considered—and it is certain—that these are of their root, and therefore it happens that they are altered through them. These are indeed all the medicines of the first order which we have brought forth; however, many methods of them can be multiplied, provided the essence of the pigmentary substances is maintained in the variety of the methods. Some, indeed, have discovered more medicines, but it necessarily happens that one of two things occurs: either it is necessary for them to create medicine from the same things or from things having the same nature, or they compose a medicine which is equivalent to what is not, along with its alteration, and which confers nothing to the world, nor to the parts of the world, until the mover in the sublime, mobile nature has rested uncorrupted.

Even in the judgment of health, one can still notice this difference. It is immediately pleasant to everyone who possesses it (at least negatively, that is, as the removal of all bodily pains). But in order to say that it is good, one must also direct it through reason toward purposes, namely, that it is a state that makes us fit for all our tasks. However, reason also struggles against this. Pleasure is enjoyment. But if one aims at this alone, it would be foolish to be scrupulous regarding the means that provide it, whether it is obtained passively, from the generosity of nature, or through activity and our own doing. But that the existence of a human being who merely lives (and is ever so busy in this intention) in order to enjoy, even if he were to best facilitate this for others who are also only out for enjoyment, because he shares all pleasure through sympathy, has a value in itself: reason will never allow itself to be persuaded of this. Only through what he does, without regard for enjoyment, in full freedom and independent of what nature could provide him even passively, does he give his existence, as the existence of a person, an absolute value; and happiness, with all the fullness of its pleasures, is by no means an unconditioned good.*)

### CHAP. 22. Concerning the principal Inca named Huayna Capac.

Huayna Capac succeeded the aforementioned Lord, a name which means wealthy or valiant youth, and he was both one and the other, more so than any of his ancestors or successors. He was very prudent and established great order throughout the land in all places. He was determined and brave, and very fortunate in war, and he achieved great victories. He extended his Kingdom much more than all his ancestors combined. Death overtook him in the Kingdom of Quito, which he had conquered, and which lies four hundred leagues from his Court. They opened him up, and his entrails and his heart remained in Quito, because he had so commanded it, and his body was brought to Cuzco and placed in the famous temple of the Sun. To this day, many buildings, paved roads, fortresses, and notable works of this King are shown; he founded the family of Tomebamba. This Huayna Capac was worshipped by his subjects as a god during his lifetime, a thing which the elders affirm was not done with any of his predecessors. When he died, they killed a thousand people from his household so that they might go to serve him in the other life, and they died with great willingness to go and serve him, so much so that many outside of those designated offered themselves for death for the same purpose. His wealth and treasure were a thing never before seen, and as the Spaniards entered shortly after his death, the Indians took great care to make it all disappear, although a large portion was taken to Cajamarca for the ransom of Atahualpa, his son. Men worthy of credit affirm that, among his sons and grandsons, he had more than three hundred in Cuzco. His mother was held in great esteem and was called Mama Ocllo. Polo <note>referring to Polo de Ondegardo, a Spanish colonial official known for collecting and burying mummies</note> sent the bodies of this woman and of Huayna Capac, highly embalmed and preserved, to Lima, and he removed an infinity of idolatries that were practiced with them. Often the weak one struggles and would like to revolt, then falls back lower than ever into servitude. Lest anyone think, therefore, that it was forbidden to sacrifice to these demons, but permitted to sacrifice to the celestial ones, or to all, or to some, He soon added: "Except to the Lord alone," that is, except to the Lord only. Lest perhaps someone, because it says "to the Lord alone," might believe that there is only one God to whom one must think sacrifice is to be offered. That this is not to be understood in that way is easily found in the Greek scriptures. Therefore, the God of the Hebrews—to whom even this philosopher gives so great a testimony—gave the law to His Hebrew people, written in the Hebrew language, not obscure and unknown, but now spread among all nations, in which law it is written: "He who sacrifices to gods shall be rooted out, except to the Lord only." What is the need in this His law and His prophets to seek out much on this matter? Indeed, there is no need to seek; for they are not hidden or rare, but manifest and frequent, and I could collect them and place them in this my disputation, by which it appears clearer than light that the true and supreme God wished sacrifice to be made to no one at all except to Himself alone. Behold this one thing, briefly, or rather grandly, menacingly, but truthfully spoken by that God whom their own most learned men preach: let it be heard, feared, and fulfilled, lest the destruction follow the disobedient. Article 3. Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

Regarding the third point, the following procedure is taken. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because those things which are prior according to nature are posterior and less known to us; but universals are prior according to the nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior relative to us, while simple things are posterior. But universals are prior, and thus they are posterior in our knowledge relative to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition prior to the parts of the definition, and those parts are less universal, just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," and universals are known later relative to us. Furthermore, effects are known to us, and principles are known later relative to us. But there is that which the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics* regarding coming to know singulars from universals. 

I answer that it must be said that two things must be considered in the cognition of our intellect. First, intellectual cognition takes its origin in some way from sensory cognition. And because sense is of singulars, and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to the cognition of universals relative to us. Second, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And what proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is the medium between potency and complete act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately. The incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as something that is in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*, things are first manifest and certain to us in a more confused way; later, however, we know things by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each of the things contained therein is to know something under a certain confusion. Thus, both the whole, in which parts are contained in potency, and the integral whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. To know distinctly that which is contained in the whole, however, is to have knowledge of a less common thing, just as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know the "animal" in which it is rational or irrational, which is to know "man" or "lion." Therefore, it occurs to our intellect to know "animal" prior to knowing "man." And if I compare it to whatever is more or less universal, just as sense exits from potency into act, so does the intellect; and this order

Or it pleases <note>the observation</note> that it is evident that a child, from the beginning, distinguishes "man" from "not-man," and in the beginning, children call all men "fathers." And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is the medium between potency and act. If, therefore, there is both sense and intellect, the cognition of the more universal is prior, and the cognition of the lesser and more common is also prior. 

To the first, it must be said that this can be considered in two ways. In one way, it can be considered according to the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the truth itself have a relationship to many things, and the abstraction of the intellect reaches this end, in this way the universal is posterior. As it is said in the first book of *De Anima*, the universal is either nothing or it is posterior. But because Plato <note>alluding to Plato's Theory of Forms</note> posited universals as substances, and in this consideration he is wrong, because particulars are nothing except through the participation of the more universal subsisting things, which are called *ideas*. In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a double order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things that are imperfect and in potency are prior. And in this way, the more universal is prior in nature, which appears manifestly in the generation of man and animal. For "animal" is generated prior to "man," as the Philosopher says in the book *De Generatione Animalium*. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as an act is simply prior in nature, because that which is perfect is prior to that which is imperfect. And in this way, the less universal is prior in nature, for nature does not rest in the generation of "animal," but it intends to generate "man." 

To the second, it must be said that the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole. And through the whole, which is made more universal, it is not only "animal" but also "man" and "horse," just as the less universal is contained not only in the more universal but also in others, like "man" not only in "animal," but also in "rational." Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition to "man." If "man" is prior in our cognition, then "animal" is so through its reason. 

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is known <unclear>partially</unclear>. In another way, when it is part of this whole, such as stones, it is necessary that we know the whole prior to the parts. For we know the house in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the definition, to be considered absolutely, is prior to the thing defined. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known through the parts of the definition, but rather the parts are what they are.

Regarding the third point, it is argued as follows. It seems that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition, because things that are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us; but universals are prior by nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composite things are prior to us compared to simple things, but universals are prior to <unclear>singulars</unclear> and are posterior in terms of being known to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first book of the *Physics* that the defined falls into our cognition prior to the parts of the definition, and those parts are less universal; for instance, "animal" is a part of the definition of "man," yet universals are known later to us. Furthermore, we encounter effects and their causes by chance, but universals are known later to us. However, it is stated in the first book of the *Physics* that we must proceed from the universal to the singular. I respond that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, intellectual cognition takes its beginning in some way from sensory cognition. And because sense is of singulars, while the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior to us than the cognition of universals. Second, we must consider that our intellect proceeds from potency to act. And what proceeds from potency to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is intermediate between potency and perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For what is known in this way is known as if in act and in a certain way in potency. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*: things are initially manifest and certain to us in a more confused way; later, however, we come to know by distinguishing principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained, without having proper knowledge of each of those things contained within it, is to know something in a certain confusion. In this way, both the whole in which the parts are contained potentially and the integral whole can be known; for both wholes can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have knowledge of a less common thing; as, for instance, knowing "animal" indistinctly, and knowing the animal in which there is rationality or irrationality, which is to know "man" or "lion." I do not write so prolixly about Alchemy in vain, but I do so with this intent and purpose, so that from these things you may know closely and solidly what lies within it, and how it ought to be understood. So precious are their secrets.

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison lies hidden and exists even in the best things? Everyone is forced to admit this. If this, therefore, is true, I ask you now: should poison not be separated from the good and useful, and the good be accepted while the evil is left behind? Indeed, it ought to be so. If, therefore, it is necessary, I pray tell me, how is that separated in your workshops? For among you, all things remain mixed. But so that you may defend your simplicity, if you are convicted of admitting that poison lies therein and are asked where it eventually goes, you then bring up I know not what regarding "corrections," which are supposed to demand and remove the poison,
<margin>The correction of physicians is scrutinized.</margin>
just as they correct Quince with Scammony, or later, Diagridium. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterward just as it was at first? And yet you boast in the meantime that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it escaped to?
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Test that, if you are wise; exceed the dose, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know that not sluggishly. Thus you also correct Turbith, and call it Diaturbith. These are your kinds of corrections, which would befit peasants and should be given to horses to drink. Make a trial by exceeding the measure, and increase the dose; you will see whether or not you are going to feel the poison.
<margin>What a physician's "correcting" is.</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected.* Whoever is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the one who was punished endures. Such are these corrections too; they are situated within the things themselves, not within you. Now, in this case, a physician must consider nothing more than that the poison be taken away. That must be done through separation: as, for example, a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted into food. If you remove the poison from it, you may eat it without harm. The same must be understood for all other things equally, namely, that a similar separation is required. Without that being done, you cannot be secure in your operation, unless it happens that nature supplies your shortcomings, or the greater benevolence of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will remain.

Now then, if that true foundation is indeed necessary—that which removes poison—how does Alchemy achieve it? For this must be done such that, if Mars is in the Sun, Mars is removed, and if Saturn is situated in Venus, it is separated from it. For as many as are the ascendants and impressions in the things of nature, so many bodies exist within them. But as for those bodies which are contrary, it is necessary that some of them be entirely removed and taken away, so that by this pact all contrariety may be lifted, and the evil which you seek may be removed from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
Just as gold is useful for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire, so Medicine is far less useful if it does not pass through fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into another generation, which ought to lead to and help man. And should this not justly be considered the proper foundation of any physician? For a physician ought not to employ poisons, but secrets.
<margin>The workshops are rebuked.</margin>
However, all those workshop preparations, as many as they are, do not contribute even a letter to this doctrine; rather, they are occupied simply with correcting, just as if a dog had broken wind in a room, and that stench were calmed either with troches and incense, or with juniper wood: I ask, does the stench not remain in the room afterward, just as it was before? And although it may not be perceived by smell, is one therefore allowed to say that the stench has been separated and remains no longer? Indeed, it is present, but "corrected" by the smoke. Thus, therefore, the smoke and the stench enter the nostrils together. Of this kind also are the corrections of the apothecaries, who dull <term>Aleopaticum</term> with sugar so that it inflicts no harm. Thus, sugar and honey are their master-art. Thus they also "correct" Gentian with theriac. Are these not the works of asinine ignorance? Yet they boast and sell themselves as the princes of physicians.
